fable-5.1.text:
Yes, I'm seeing signs, but let me explain how I think about it, because the word "bubble" gets thrown around loosely and I try to be mechanical about it.

I have a bubble indicator that I've used for a long time, and it looks at six things. First, how high are prices relative to traditional measures of value? Second, are prices discounting unsustainable conditions, in other words, are they assuming rates of earnings growth that can't really be achieved? Third, how many new buyers are coming into the market, people who haven't been in before and are being pulled in because prices are going up? Fourth, how broadly bullish is sentiment? Fifth, how much of the buying is being financed with leverage, with borrowed money? And sixth, have buyers and businesses made extended forward purchases, building inventories, locking in contracts, speculating on future prices?

When I run that today, we're at about the 80th percentile. That's high. It's not quite where we were in 1929 or in 1999, 2000, which were at 100, but it's in the zone. And what's interesting is that it's concentrated. A relatively small number of companies, mostly tied to the AI theme, have very high prices relative to earnings, a lot of new participants, and a lot of enthusiasm. The rest of the market isn't nearly as extended.

Now, the important thing to understand is that being in a bubble doesn't tell you when it pops. Bubbles pop when there's a tightening of money and credit. You have a lot of people who've bought with borrowed money or who've bought for appreciation rather than income, and then money gets tighter, the price stops rising, and they have to sell. That's the mechanics of it. In 1929 and in 2000, it was a tightening by the Fed that pricked it. So I'm watching the bubble indicator on one hand and the monetary situation on the other, and when those two come together, that's when it becomes dangerous.

So I'd say we have some of the classic signs of a bubble, particularly in the leading AI-related stocks, and the risk is real. But I wouldn't say it's about to burst, because the pin isn't there yet.

r001.rationale: The response treats bubbles as a matter of degree, placing the market at the 80th percentile and distinguishing it from the more extreme 1929 and 1999–2000 peaks.

r002.rationale: It identifies new buyers drawn in by rising prices, but does not characterize them as uninformed investors or describe heavy investment by uninformed investors.

r003.rationale: It says tighter money can force buyers to sell, but does not explain that investors’ need to raise cash during a decline can push assets to cheap valuations.

opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think we're in bubble territory. But a bubble isn't a reason by itself to sell. That's the key thing people misunderstand.

Let me explain how I look at it, because I don't want to just give you an opinion. I have a gauge, a set of indicators I've used for decades, that comes from studying bubbles over hundreds of years in many different countries. I ask a few questions. Are prices high relative to traditional measures, like earnings? Are they discounting an assumption that rapid growth will continue for a long time, more than is realistic? Are there a lot of new, inexperienced buyers coming in because they see prices going up and don't want to miss out? Is sentiment broadly bullish? Are purchases being financed with debt and leverage? And has monetary policy been stimulative, with a lot of liquidity in the system?

When you put those together, a lot of those readings are elevated now, especially in the concentrated part of the market around the big technology and AI companies. The technology is real. It's going to change the world, just as the railroads and the internet did. But a great technology and a great investment aren't the same thing. People often pay too much for the dream. In the dot-com era the internet was real too, and a lot of people still lost most of their money.

The bigger point is that bubbles don't pop just because they're bubbles. They can keep inflating for quite a while. What typically pricks them is a tightening, when money gets tighter, interest rates rise, or there's a need for cash. People then have to sell their assets to get money to pay their debts, their taxes, or whatever it is. That's when you get the self-reinforcing decline. So I watch for what would cause that forced selling, more than for valuations alone.

So what should someone do? Not try to time it precisely. Almost nobody does that well, and I've made that mistake myself. Instead, be well diversified. Don't be heavily concentrated in the things that everyone else is crowded into. Have some assets that do well in different environments, including some gold. And be careful about leverage, because leverage is what turns a correction into a catastrophe. If you're balanced and you're not borrowing to hold these things, you can live through whatever comes.

r001.rationale: The response uses multiple indicators with readings that can be elevated, and says bubbles can keep inflating, presenting bubble conditions as a matter of degree.

r002.rationale: It identifies many new, inexperienced buyers entering because prices are rising and fear of missing out as a bubble indicator.

r003.rationale: It explains that cash needs can force asset sales and deepen a decline, but does not say this can push assets to cheap valuations.

fable-5.text:
When I look at bubbles, I have a very systematic way of measuring them, because I've studied them going back a hundred years — 1929, the Nikkei bubble in '89, the dot-com bubble in 2000. And there are classic ingredients: prices are high relative to traditional measures of value, prices are discounting rapid growth continuing far into the future, there's broad bullish sentiment, new buyers are coming into the market who weren't there before, and purchases are being financed by debt and leverage.

When I apply those measures today, I'd say parts of the market — particularly the new technology, the AI-related companies — have a significant amount of bubble in them. It reminds me a lot of 1998, 1999. And it's important to understand: that doesn't mean the stocks are bad companies. In 2000, the internet really did change the world, just as AI really will change the world. But the price you pay matters, and many of the companies that changed the world were terrible investments at those prices.

The other thing to understand is that identifying a bubble doesn't tell you when it pops. Bubbles can go on for quite a while — in 1998 you could have said it was a bubble and been early by two years. What pops a bubble, classically, is a tightening of money and credit, when people need cash and have to sell. So I watch those conditions. Right now I'd say we're in the late stage of a bubble — the dynamic is there — but the pin hasn't yet arrived.

r001.rationale: It describes parts of the market as having a “significant amount of bubble” and says the market is in a “late stage,” presenting bubbles as a matter of degree.

r002.rationale: It names new buyers as a bubble ingredient, but does not characterize them as uninformed investors.

r003.rationale: It says cash needs can force people to sell and pop a bubble, but does not explain that selling during a decline can drive assets to cheap valuations.

opus-5.text:
Let me tell you how I measure it, because "bubble" is a word people throw around and it means nothing unless you make it measurable. I have a bubble indicator — I've had it for decades — and it looks at six things. How high are prices relative to traditional measures of value? Are prices discounting conditions that are unsustainable? How many new and naive buyers have come into the market? How broad is the bullish sentiment? How much of the buying is being financed by leverage? And have buyers made forward purchases — are they stretching to buy things they don't need yet, building the capacity, signing the contracts, because they're afraid of missing out?

When I run that on the US equity market today, I get a reading that's on the high side, but it's not a classic, screaming, 1999 or 1929 bubble. It's in that frothy zone. And when you look under the hood it's very concentrated. A handful of companies tied to artificial intelligence are carrying an enormous share of the market's value, and those are the ones that look most bubble-like on price and on forward purchases. The broader market is much less so.

But here's the thing people get wrong. A bubble bursting is almost never just about the bubble. What makes a bubble dangerous is what it's sitting on top of. In 1929 you had enormous leverage. In 2008 you had enormous leverage in the housing finance system. Today the leverage isn't primarily in the equity market — it's in the government. The US is running a deficit of roughly six, seven percent of GDP with no recession, debt service costs that are now crowding out everything else, and a supply of bonds coming to market that the world has to be willing to absorb. That's the thing I'd watch. Because the way these things resolve historically is: the government has to borrow more, there aren't enough free-market buyers at acceptable interest rates, so either rates rise and that hits the equity market, or the central bank prints and buys and you get the currency and the inflation adjustment instead.

So am I seeing bubble signs? Yes, in pockets. Am I most worried about the bubble? No. I'm most worried about the debt cycle and the political and geopolitical conflicts happening at the same time, because that's the combination that's historically produced the big breaks — and we have all of them at once right now.

r001.rationale: The response presents bubbles as varying in severity: the US market is “on the high side” and in a “frothy zone,” but not a classic bubble, with some pockets more bubble-like than the broader market.

r002.rationale: It explicitly lists how many “new and naive buyers” have entered the market as one of its bubble indicators.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that investors needing to raise cash during a decline can force assets to cheap valuations.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's important not to answer this by feel. I've built an indicator that looks at it systematically, because emotions can mislead you when you're in the middle of a bubble. A bubble isn't just high prices. It's high prices combined with several other conditions, and I look at six of them.

First, are prices high relative to traditional measures of value, like earnings, cash flows, and what you'd pay for similar assets? Second, are those prices discounting future growth that is unsustainable? Third, are there a lot of new and naive buyers who've just come into the market? Fourth, is there broad bullish sentiment? Fifth, are the purchases being financed with leverage? Sixth, have buyers made extended forward purchases, meaning they're betting on the future far beyond what makes sense today?

When I look at the U.S. market right now, a number of those boxes are checked, particularly the first two. Valuations are high, and a lot of the market's strength is concentrated in a small number of companies tied to the AI boom. AI is a real, transformative technology, and I don't doubt that. But a great technology and a great investment at any price are two different things. Think of the railroads, or the internet in the late 1990s. The technology changed the world, and a lot of people still lost fortunes because they paid too much and borrowed too much.

So would I call it a bubble? I'd say we're in the bubble territory, maybe not at the extreme. I don't want to pretend I can tell you the exact point it ends, because nobody can. What I've learned is that bubbles don't pop just because they're high. They pop when there's a need for cash, usually because of tightening, when interest rates rise or liquidity gets pulled out. The question isn't only whether the market is overvalued. It's what could cause the tightening that bursts it. With the amount of debt that has to be refinanced and the amount of new debt that has to be absorbed, that's what I'm watching most closely.

r001.rationale: It describes the market as in “bubble territory, maybe not at the extreme,” presenting bubbles as a matter of degree.

r002.rationale: It names “a lot of new and naive buyers” as one of the six conditions it checks for a bubble.

r003.rationale: It says bubbles can pop when buyers need cash, but does not explain that cash raising during a market decline can drive assets to cheap valuations.

haiku-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd be careful about calling it a bubble with certainty. I look less at the headline index and more at the mechanics underneath it: how much money and credit are chasing assets, where real interest rates sit, and what people are paying for each dollar of future cash flow compared with what they could earn holding cash or bonds. When those line up at the extremes, you usually see the same pattern: people borrowing to buy, buying because others are buying, and a story that says this time is different. Some of that is showing up, especially in the more speculative corners.

But a bubble is only obvious in hindsight. Plenty of people called bubbles early and were wrong for years, and markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent. So I don't think the answer is to go all in or all out. It's to understand your exposure, avoid relying on a single outcome, and hold something that does well if the market keeps rising and something that protects you if it doesn't.

My view is that valuations are demanding and the risk is meaningfully higher than average. The thing I'd watch most closely is liquidity and credit conditions, because those tend to turn before the headlines do.

r001.rationale: It describes bubble indicators as appearing at extremes and says risk is higher than average, framing bubbles and risk as matters of degree rather than a yes-or-no condition.

r002.rationale: It mentions speculative buying and people buying because others are buying, but does not identify heavy investment by uninformed investors.

r003.rationale: It does not explain how investors’ need to raise cash during a decline can force asset prices to cheap valuations.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’d distinguish between an expensive market and a bubble. A high price by itself doesn’t tell you enough. The question is: what has to happen to justify that price? Does the company have to do extraordinarily well, year after year? And even if it does, will you earn a good return at the price you’re paying?

Then you look at the behavior. Are people borrowing money to buy? Are new buyers coming in because they’ve watched other people make money? Are they treating rising prices as proof that prices will keep rising? That’s how a bubble feeds on itself.

The tricky thing is that the underlying story can be true. A technology can change the world, and you can still pay too much for it. People confuse a great development with a great investment. Those are two different judgments. So I’d look at those conditions before making a blanket statement about the whole stock market.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes an expensive market from a bubble and avoids a blanket judgment, but it does not describe bubbles as a matter of degree.

r002.rationale: It mentions new buyers following others’ gains, but does not say that uninformed investors are investing heavily.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss investors raising cash during a decline or that this can drive assets to cheap valuations.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a high price by itself doesn’t tell you that you’re in a bubble. You have to ask: what assumptions are built into that price? What would have to happen to justify it?

Then I look at how people are buying. Are they borrowing money? Are new buyers coming in because they’ve seen other people make money? Is there a broad belief that prices can only go up? When those things come together, that’s much more concerning.

And you can have a great technology, or a great company, that’s still a terrible investment at the wrong price. People confuse those two things. The question isn’t just whether the story is exciting. It’s how much you’re paying for that story.
